chunks: "A pull-up or pull-down is necessary whenever a node could otherwise be undriven.
Floating inputs: a button that is open some of the time, an input from a chip that might be tri-stated, an unused pin.
Open-drain outputs: the pull-up is what makes the line go high at all, so I2C, shared interrupts and resets.

And things that must have a safe default while the MCU boots: a MOSFET gate needs a pull-down so the load stays off, an enable or chip-select needs a pull-up so the device stays idle, boot-strap pins need a defined level at reset.
Sizing is a trade-off between two limits.
Too big a resistor and it's weak: leakage current times R shifts the level, the RC with the pin and trace capacitance slows the edge, and it's easy for noise to overpower.
Too small and it wastes current every time the line is pulled the other way, 3. 3 volts over 1 kilohms is 3.
3 milliamps, and a driver may not be able to sink that while staying below its low-level voltage. So I compute both bounds. For a button, 10 kilohms: 0.
33 milliamps only while pressed, a clean edge, and leakage effects negligible. For I2C at 400 kilohertz with 100 picofarads, the maximum is about 3.
5 kilohms for rise time, and the minimum is about 1 kilohms from a 3 milliamps sink at 0. 4 volts, so 2. 2 to 3. 3 kilohms.
For a MOSFET gate pull-down, 100 kilohms is typical, with the gate capacitance setting turn-off time."
